content:
Former Liberal minister Philip Ruddock has been appointed by the Australian cabinet to review whether current laws adequately protect the right to religious freedom. The appointment, announced on Wednesday, is intended to defuse a contentious debate over religious amendments being proposed as part of a same-sex marriage bill.

***

The move comes amid divisions within the government. Senior conservatives like Peter Dutton and Mathias Cormann have suggested that a religious freedom bill can be addressed separately next year, while others, including Treasurer Scott Morrison and Senator David Fawcett, have insisted that religious protections must be considered alongside the marriage bill. Morrison stated that the review was "no substitute" for including those amendments now.

***

Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull emphasized the need to approach religious freedom carefully in the wake of the yes vote on marriage equality. He noted that many of the proposals put forward in recent months extend well beyond the immediate issue of marriage, and warned parliament to be cautious of unintended consequences when legislating protections for fundamental rights.

***

Turnbull expressed particular concern about the risks of broadly worded, bill of rights-style declarations, stating that any reforms to protect religious freedom should be undertaken with care. He described the review as a "timely expert stocktake" to guide any necessary legislative changes. Ruddock has been asked to deliver his report by 31 March.

***

Turnbull said Ruddock was well suited for the role, citing his experience as Australia's special envoy for human rights. The review is seen as an effort to balance the advancement of marriage equality with the protection of religious freedoms, while managing competing demands from within the government.
